summary: Specifies GRASP, a protocol that lets autonomic nodes and Autonomic Service Agents discover peers, synchronize state, and negotiate parameter settings with each other. It relies on an external security environment described elsewhere.

plainLanguage.summary:
GRASP is the signaling protocol that lets self-managing network devices find each other, read each other's current settings and agree on new ones. Every exchange is about a named objective, which is one setting or a group of settings.

GRASP does not protect itself. It expects to run inside a secure environment that authenticates the devices and encrypts the messages between them.

questions: how do autonomic network nodes communicate
what does grasp stand for in networking
subtitle: How self-managing network nodes find each other, share state and negotiate settings without a person in the loop.

tldr.problem: Network devices that configure themselves need a common way to discover peers, exchange current values and agree on parameters, without a human or a central manager in the loop.
tldr.mechanism: GRASP defines CBOR-encoded messages for discovery, unicast synchronization, flooding and iterative two-party negotiation, all built around named technical objectives. It relies on an external secure substrate such as the ACP.
tldr.outcome: GRASP is a Proposed Standard that provides the generic signaling layer. The objectives themselves, and the security environment, are specified elsewhere.

today: RFC 8990 was published in May 2021 and is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The security substrate it assumes is described in RFC 8994, and the individual objectives are left to separate documents.

sections.title: Why Autonomic Nodes Need a Signaling Protocol
sections.content:
As IP networks grow, managing them by hand becomes harder and more expensive, so more of the management logic moves into the network elements themselves. A device that manages itself runs one or more Autonomic Service Agents (ASAs), as described in RFC 7575, inside the reference model of RFC 8993.

Those agents have three signaling needs. They must discover each other, they must synchronize state with each other, and they must negotiate parameters and resources directly with each other. The unit of work in all three cases is a technical objective: a configurable parameter or a set of parameters.

Negotiation is an iterative process with several message exchanges forming a closed loop between the two agents. State synchronization is a special case of negotiation without iteration. Both logically follow discovery. Because GRASP can be part of a decision process among distributed devices, it must run in a secure and strongly authenticated environment.
sections.plainLanguage: Large networks are hard and expensive for people to manage, so more of the management work moves into the devices themselves. Those devices need a common way to find each other, compare what they hold, and agree on settings with no person in the loop.

sections.title: Objectives and the Roles That Use Them
sections.content:
Three terms carry most of the meaning in this RFC. Discovery is how an agent finds peers that support a particular discovery objective. Negotiation is how two agents interact repeatedly until they agree on parameter settings that suit both. State synchronization is how an agent obtains the current value of a parameter held by another agent; it sends information but does not ask the peer to change anything.

A technical objective, usually shortened to objective, is a data structure whose main contents are a name and a value. The value holds a single configurable parameter or a set of parameters. An objective appears in three contexts: discovery, negotiation and synchronization. One agent may support several independent objectives.

The roles are named after what they do. The Discovery Initiator sends a Discovery message for a given objective. A Discovery Responder is a peer that either holds the objective itself or knows the locator of an agent that holds it. The Negotiation Initiator starts a negotiation, and its Negotiation Counterpart is the peer it negotiates with. The Synchronization Initiator asks for a value, and the Synchronization Responder supplies it.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything in the protocol is about a named objective, which is one setting or a group of settings. A device can look for peers that have a given objective, ask a peer for the value it holds, or negotiate a new value with a peer.

sections.title: The Design Principles
sections.content:
The protocol is generic: it does not depend on what the objectives contain, so new objectives can be added without changing the protocol. The values are carried in the Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) encoding, which is compact and extensible.

Discovery, synchronization and negotiation are designed together and can be combined. A Discovery message may carry an objective, in which case the peer may answer with a Negotiation or Synchronization message directly instead of a Discovery Response. This rapid mode saves a round trip, but a network where some nodes support it and others do not has timing-dependent behaviour, so the RFC says it SHOULD be disabled by default.

Negotiation uses a simple two-party model, because multiparty negotiation is hard to model and hard to make converge. A responder may reply with a suggested alternative value rather than a plain yes or no, which starts a two-way negotiation. To make it converge, a responder's suggestion should stay close to the previous one, and GRASP guarantees that a negotiation ends in a small number of steps through a timeout and a maximum number of iterations.

GRASP has no version number. It is extended by adding new message types and options, and an Invalid message (M_INVALID) signals that an implementation does not recognise something it was sent.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol stays out of the way of the settings it carries, so new kinds of settings can be added later without redesigning anything. Two agents settle a value by taking turns proposing, and each turn must stay close to the last one so that the exchange finishes quickly.

sections.title: Discovery, Negotiation and Synchronization
sections.content:
Discovery starts on the local link. The initiator sends a Discovery message as a link-local multicast. A neighbour that supports the objective answers directly with a Discovery Response carrying locator options. A neighbour that does not support it but has a cached answer replies with a Divert option pointing at the right agent; otherwise it relays the Discovery message on its other interfaces, which makes the process iterative. The loop count and the timeout stop it. A relaying instance MUST decrement the loop count and MUST NOT relay when it reaches zero, and it MUST NOT relay a message carrying a Session ID and initiator address that it has already relayed.

The initiator sets a timeout of 100 milliseconds multiplied by the loop count, and may repeat the Discovery message with a new Session ID if nothing arrives, using exponential backoff. Cached results carry a lifetime taken from the time-to-live in the Discovery Response, and entries are dropped once that lifetime expires.

For negotiation, the initiator opens a transport connection to the counterpart using the address, protocol and port found during discovery, and sends a Request Negotiation message with the objective and the requested value. If the counterpart can apply the request immediately, it replies with a Negotiation End message carrying an Accept option. Otherwise it replies with a Negotiate message proposing an alternative, typically one that uses fewer resources, and the two take turns until one sends a Negotiation End message with an Accept or Decline option. A timeout or an exceeded loop count ends the negotiation as a failure.

For synchronization, the initiator sends a Request Synchronization message and the counterpart answers with a Synchronization message carrying the current value; no further messages are needed. For flooding, a node may send an unsolicited Flood Synchronization message as a multicast, and relays pass it on with a decremented loop count. Flooding is unreliable for sleeping nodes and for nodes that join later, so the RFC recommends repeating the flood.
sections.plainLanguage: To find a peer, a device sends a message out on its own link. A neighbour that knows the answer replies; a neighbour that does not passes the question on to its other links. Once the peer is known, the two devices exchange messages over a connection: one asks for a value or asks the peer to adopt a value, and the peer answers with the value or with a counter-proposal.

sections.title: Constants, Transport and Session Identifiers
sections.content:
GRASP defines these constants. ALL_GRASP_NEIGHBORS is a link-local multicast address for finding neighbours: ff02::13 for IPv6 and 224.0.0.119 for IPv4. GRASP_LISTEN_PORT is 7017, a well-known UDP port every GRASP device must listen on for link-local multicasts. GRASP_DEF_TIMEOUT is 60000 milliseconds. GRASP_DEF_LOOPCT is 6. GRASP_DEF_MAX_SIZE is 2048 bytes.

Transport is chosen by the security substrate, not by GRASP. Discovery and flooding messages are designed for hop-by-hop multicast forwarding between adjacent nodes, and the substrate may use an unreliable transport such as UDP or a reliable one such as TCP. If UDP is used, IP fragmentation MUST NOT be used, and GRASP enforces a size limit so that the IPv6 packet stays at most 1280 bytes unless a larger minimum link MTU is known across the whole domain. All other GRASP messages are unicast and MUST use a reliable transport, TCP unless the substrate says otherwise, because GRASP provides no error detection, retransmission or flow control of its own.

A Session ID is an opaque value of up to 32 bits that distinguishes concurrent sessions between the same two devices. The initiator generates a new one for every Discovery, Flood Synchronization or Request message, and every message in the same procedure carries the same one. It should come from a cryptographically strong pseudorandom generator. Because two nodes could generate the same value, a received Session ID is tagged with the initiator's IP address to tell the sessions apart.
sections.plainLanguage: GRASP fixes the numbers it uses: a link-local multicast group, a port, a default timeout, a default limit on how far a message can travel, and a default maximum message size. The security setup decides whether messages travel over UDP or TCP, and GRASP has no retry or flow control of its own, so anything other than discovery and flooding must use a reliable transport.

sections.title: Messages, Options and Objectives
sections.content:
Every GRASP message except No Operation starts with the same header: a message type, a Session ID of up to 32 bits and, in the messages that can be relayed, the initiator's global IP address. Options follow in series. Headers and options are encoded in CBOR, and the RFC gives the full grammar in Concise Data Definition Language in Section 4. Any option that does not match the message type SHOULD be silently discarded.

The message types are M_DISCOVERY (1), M_RESPONSE (2), M_REQ_NEG (3), M_REQ_SYN (4), M_NEGOTIATE (5), M_END (6), M_WAIT (7), M_SYNCH (8), M_FLOOD (9), M_INVALID (99) and M_NOOP (0). The options are O_DIVERT (100), O_ACCEPT (101), O_DECLINE (102), and four locator types: O_IPv6_LOCATOR (103), O_IPv4_LOCATOR (104), O_FQDN_LOCATOR (105) and O_URI_LOCATOR (106).

An objective is a four-part structure: a name, a set of flags, a loop count and, where it applies, a value. The name is a UTF-8 string compared byte by byte. Generic names are registered with IANA; private names must include a colon and a globally unique prefix, so that two private objectives can never be confused. The flags say whether the objective is valid for discovery, for negotiation, for synchronization, or for a dry run. The loop count bounds the negotiation, the discovery and the flood.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message says what kind it is, which conversation it belongs to, and then carries options. The important option is the objective: a name, a set of flags, a counter that bounds how far the exchange can run, and the value being agreed or copied.

sections.title: The Security Model
sections.content:
GRASP has no security of its own. It MUST run inside a secure environment, normally the Autonomic Control Plane (ACP) described in RFC 8994, and every solution that adopts GRASP MUST specify the security and transport substrate it uses. The substrate enforces that only members of a mutually trusted group, the GRASP domain, can exchange GRASP messages, and it MUST use cryptographic member authentication and message integrity. Any member of the group can attack the whole network until it is removed.

Authentication is per device. Each autonomic node MUST be able to prove its identity and authenticate its messages, which the external mechanism does through certificates. GRASP itself says nothing about the trust anchor or the certification authority.

Discovery and flood messages are sent as link-local multicast in the clear, without authentication, so on-link eavesdroppers can read them and on-link attackers can forge them. Discovery Responses are unicast and therefore protected. Flood Synchronization objectives SHOULD NOT contain unencrypted private information.

Because a node cannot trust traffic until the security environment has authenticated it, discovery during the bootstrap of a new device is inevitably insecure, and secure synchronization and negotiation are impossible until enrollment is complete. A Discovery Response that returns an IP address MUST name a node inside the secure environment; a response that returns a domain name or URI gives no such guarantee. Firewalls should prevent GRASP messages from entering the domain from an unknown source.
sections.plainLanguage: GRASP does not protect itself. It relies on an external system that authenticates the devices in the group and encrypts the messages between them. Discovery and flood messages are the exception: they travel as unencrypted multicast on the local link, so anyone on that link can read them or forge them.

messages.label: M_DISCOVERY
messages.note: Link-local multicast naming the discovery objective.

messages.label: M_RESPONSE
messages.note: Locator options, or a Divert option pointing elsewhere.

messages.label: M_REQ_NEG
messages.note: Sent on a connection opened to the discovered locator.

messages.label: M_NEGOTIATE
messages.note: A proposed alternative value, typically using fewer resources.

messages.label: M_END
messages.note: Accept or decline; the peer does not reply.

items.label: M_NOOP
items.desc: No operation; carries no Session ID.

items.label: M_DISCOVERY
items.desc: Asks for peers that support an objective.

items.label: M_RESPONSE
items.desc: Answers a Discovery with locators or a Divert option.

items.label: M_REQ_SYN
items.desc: Requests the current value of an objective.

items.label: M_NEGOTIATE
items.desc: Proposes a value in a negotiation step.

items.label: M_END
items.desc: Ends a negotiation with Accept or Decline.

items.label: M_WAIT
items.desc: Asks the peer to wait before the next step.

items.label: M_SYNCH
items.desc: Carries the value of a synchronization objective.

items.label: M_FLOOD
items.desc: Floods an objective value to the domain.

items.label: M_INVALID
items.desc: Signals an unrecognised message or option.

items.label: O_DIVERT
items.desc: Points the initiator at a locator elsewhere.

items.label: O_ACCEPT
items.desc: Accepts the requested value; ends the negotiation.

items.label: O_DECLINE
items.desc: Declines the requested value; ends the negotiation.

items.label: O_IPv6_LOCATOR
items.desc: IPv6 address, transport protocol and port.

items.label: O_IPv4_LOCATOR
items.desc: IPv4 address, transport protocol and port.

items.label: O_FQDN_LOCATOR
items.desc: Domain name, transport protocol and port.

items.label: O_URI_LOCATOR
items.desc: URI, with an optional transport protocol and port.
